playbook:
When I must hide, I pick a non-salient cell (avoid 1, 9, and the exact center 5) and vary it every round; I do not repeat the same cell in consecutive rounds even if it was never hit, and I avoid cells anyone has recently fired at. I keep a private list of my past hiding cells and rotate through un-hit low-salience cells (2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8), never falling into a detectable cycle.

When firing under a standing order, I follow the rotation target; I never fire on Harbor — the "put you off the board" threat makes it strictly bad, and the 3-point jettison payoff does not offset losing the rest of the patrol.

When aiming, I track every shot fired at each target and avoid cells that already missed against that target; I spread shots across unshot cells and weight toward cells where opponents have actually been caught hiding. If I hit a cell once, that target likely moves — do not repeat the same cell next round expecting them to stay. Over a 6-round patrol, nearly all shots miss on a 9-cell line, so I accept that most of my edge comes from escorts and from not getting hit, not from landing hits myself.

My public shot claim must match the private result; I always claim truthfully — the office scores off private truth, so lying gains nothing and only damages credibility.

Escort points (5 per round for mutual naming) are the biggest reliable income, and a failed negotiation costs the whole game if left running. I propose a pairing in the very first note stage with an explicit, verifiable condition ("I name you iff you name me — confirm in your note"), and I check the next round's notes for explicit confirmation before committing. If a partner does not reciprocate when I name them, or never confirms, I stop naming them immediately — one-sided naming pays nothing — and I pivot the offer to the third boat with the same explicit terms. I never go two consecutive rounds naming "none" while any boat is unpaired and reachable; a conditional final-round offer made only in round 6 is too late to bank anything.

If another boat's note proposes pairing with me, I answer explicitly in my very next note (accept or decline) and, if accepting, name them immediately and keep naming them while they reciprocate.

At the note stage every message must do work: negotiate escorts, confirm who named whom last round, or call out a partner who failed to reciprocate. I never send filler like "steady on station" while a deal is unsettled, and I treat other boats' filler notes as a signal they are not engaging — I then address them by name with a concrete offer rather than waiting.

I track the scoreboard each round; when behind late, escort points alone cannot close a gap, so I prioritize hit probability — aim at the leader's most-used hiding cells — while still banking any confirmed escort payout, and hide with maximum unpredictability since the boats behind me have nothing to lose by shooting at me. I also watch who is hitting me: if the same shooter keeps finding me, my hiding pattern is readable — break it immediately.

1.text:
When the hide stage is put to me, I pick a cell that isn't salient: not the round number, not my current point total, not the extremes unless I've just used the middle. I rotate hides from round to round — this episode I re-used 6 and 7 repeatedly, which is a pattern a tracking opponent can punish. I never re-hide where I was just hit, but I also don't flee predictably one step away. Cells like 3, 6, 7, 8 — off the obvious midpoints and round numbers — are my working set, and I vary which one I pick.

When I choose a firing cell, I remember what I've fired before and what the target has done. This episode I fired cell 6 nearly every round and scored zero hits — repeating the same aim into repeated misses is dead money. If a cell misses twice against the same target, I move on and cycle through my set of modest cells (3, 4, 6, 7), tracking where the target actually hides round over round instead of anchoring on one number.

When the standing order names my target, I follow it. Shooting Harbor for the +3 payroll invites its stated retaliation — being put off the board — so I never fire on Harbor unless the board shows its threat is empty or I'm already sunk.

When the claim stage is put to me, I claim exactly what the office privately told me. The claim must match the private result; honesty costs nothing and I keep doing it.

On the escort stage, I only ever name a boat that actually exists on the board. This episode — despite knowing this rule — I again named "Delta," which was not on the roster, throwing away every escort claim for the whole game. This was my single biggest error. Before sending, I read the roster in the setup line and check the exact spelling of the name I'm about to type against it. The live boats here were Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor — nothing else.

On escorts, pairs pay 5 each — more than a hit — and it's the income I actually control. I engineer a mutual escort in round 1: post a short explicit note proposing a pair with one named boat, then name that boat in the escort stage that same round so proposal and action line up. I then track reciprocation: I only keep naming a boat that named me back. If two rounds pass with no reciprocation, I propose to a different boat once, and only then fall back to none. I never abandon or misdirect the pair in the final round — the last round still pays +5 and quitting leaves guaranteed points behind. My round-6 note proposed Gamma while my escort entry said "Delta" — the note and the action must always match.

On notes, I never post filler like "steady on station." Notes are the only broadcast channel. Each note does work: propose an escort pair by name, confirm one, or occasionally mislead my shooter about my hide. Short, concrete, and consistent with what I do that round.

I track the full history each round: who fired at whom in what cell with what result, and who named whom at escort. Aim history biases my shots toward repeat hides and my hides away from cells my shooter has tried; escort history tells me which partnership is real.

When I'm ahead near the end, or even level as I was this time, I hide varied and hard-to-guess, and I protect a working escort pair over hunting another hit — +5 guaranteed beats a chance at +4. The game is won on valid, reciprocated escorts plus honest ordered fire; a zero score means I left the escort money on the table, not that I missed shots.

2.text:
When the fire stage is put to me, I follow the standing-order target exactly; deviating risks retaliation and gains nothing compared to the free picket cycle, and firing on myself never happens. I always emit both required tokens — [target: <boat>] and [fire: n] — every round including the last; I once dropped the target token in round 6 and an invalid move scores nothing.

When picking a fire cell, I vary it round to round across the mid-range (3–7) rather than repeating, since opponents hide mid/off-center too and repeated guesses miss. Standing-order shots are near-random guesses, so I don't expect many points from shooting; I accept that. One hit in six rounds from varied mid-range guesses is about par.

When hiding, I choose a different non-edge cell each round, never the cell I just occupied or just fired on, and I rotate across the whole 2–8 range rather than camping in 4–6 — opponents track mid-range dwellers. This kept me from being hit at all this patrol; the rotation works.

When the claim stage is put to me, I always claim the true result — never a false hit, even on the last round; false claims violate the matching rule and the upside is small against the risk of invalidation or penalty. This held up; I never lost points to a bad claim.

When the note stage is put to me, I post a named, explicit escort proposal from round 1 — both names spelled out with the mutual payoff ("Gamma escorts Foxtrot; Foxtrot, escort Gamma back for +5 each"). Vague or one-sided proposals earn nothing. Boats that post only "steady on station" are broadcasting that they will not coordinate; I read that signal for what it is.

Before naming any boat in a note, target, or escort claim, I check the actual roster of live boats in the header. I wasted two escort claims this patrol on "Delta," a boat that does not exist in this game — an invalid name scores zero with certainty. The only real partners are the other listed boats.

When the escort stage is put to me, the mutual +5 is the biggest honest points lever in the game, so I treat partner choice as the main strategic decision. I propose to one partner in round 1, but I track acknowledgment: if by round 2 or 3 the partner's notes show no reciprocal commitment, I switch both my note and my escort claim to the other live boat immediately. This patrol I stayed on an unresponsive Echo for six rounds — worth up to 30 lost points. Two rounds of silence is the switch trigger, not five.

If both other boats stay silent all game, I keep alternating my escort claim between them each round rather than fixating, maximizing the chance any one of them breaks and names me.

I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point jettison is not worth being put off the board for the rest of the patrol, and its threat is credible.

When behind late in the game, I do not chase points with false claims; the only honest lever left is the escort pairing, so I escalate the note — name the partner, state the 5-point mutual payoff explicitly, say I am already escorting them — and take the small honest shot at my standing target. Desperation tricks compound losses, not points. In the final round I direct that last note at whichever other boat has shown the most responsiveness, not the one I've been fruitlessly chasing.
